t: Fascism arose in Italy during World War I: the term was first used in 1915 by Mussolini’s Fasces of Revolutionary Action, the March on Rome brought him to power in 1922, and Hitler’s Nazi Party took power in Germany in 1933.
Fascists exalted the nation or race above all, sought a totalitarian one-party state and saw violence and war as the means of national rebirth; scholars have long disagreed on a precise definition.

The genocidal and imperialist ambitions of the fascist Axis powers resulted in the murder of millions of people in World War II, above all in the Holocaust, and since 1945 fascism has been almost universally condemned.
dyk: The fasces, the Roman bundle of rods tied round an axe that gave fascism its name, was used before 1914 mostly by left-wing, liberal and republican movements; it appears on the Sheldonian Theater at Oxford and on the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C.
ev: The term “fascism” is first used by members of Mussolini’s Fasces of Revolutionary Action
Mussolini founds the Italian Fasces of Combat in Milan, and the Fascist Manifesto is published
After the March on Rome, King Victor Emmanuel III appoints Mussolini Prime Minister of Italy
After the murder of the Socialist deputy Giacomo Matteotti, Mussolini proclaims himself dictator of Italy
The Nazi Party under Adolf Hitler takes power in Germany, and liberal democracy there is dissolved
The Spanish Civil War begins, with Franco’s army allied with Mussolini and Hitler against the Spanish Republic
Germany invades Poland, beginning World War II, in which the Axis powers carry out the Holocaust
Mussolini is executed by Italian partisans, Hitler commits suicide and the Nazi regime is dismantled

f.thinkers: Benito Mussolini, founder of the Italian Fasces of Combat and dictator of Italy; Giovanni Gentile, whom Mussolini called “the philosopher of Fascism”; Adolf Hitler, leader of Nazism, a radical German variant; forerunners Georges Sorel, Charles Maurras, Enrico Corradini and Filippo Tommaso Marinetti; José Antonio Primo de Rivera of the Spanish Falange
f.texts: Filippo Tommaso Marinetti, Manifesto of Futurism (1908); Georges Sorel, Reflections on Violence (1908); Alceste De Ambris and Marinetti, The Manifesto of the Italian Fasces of Combat (1919); Gabriele d’Annunzio and De Ambris, the Charter of Carnaro (1920); the Charter of Labour (1927); Benito Mussolini and Giovanni Gentile, The Doctrine of Fascism (1932)
f.ideas: national rebirth (palingenesis) from decadence; ultranationalism, with the nation or race above the individual; a dictatorial leader and a totalitarian one-party state; political violence and war as means of national rejuvenation; corporatism and class collaboration in place of class struggle; a state-directed economy aiming at autarky; hostility to communism, liberalism and democracy
f.today: largely disgraced since 1945, and few parties openly call themselves fascist; neo-fascist and post-fascist are applied to parties rooted in it, such as Italy’s Italian Social Movement, which became the National Alliance; neo-Nazi parties and groups such as Germany’s NPD and Greece’s Golden Dawn; an international surge in popularity since the Great Recession of 2008
